variants.name: ASP.NET Core request-delegate pipeline
variants.idiom_name: app.Use(...) with RequestDelegate next.Invoke(context), terminated by app.Run
variants.implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core already implements the pattern: `app.Use` appends a middleware component to an ordered request pipeline, every component receives the next `RequestDelegate` and either calls `await next.Invoke(context)` or ends the response and returns, which makes it the terminal middleware (`app.Run` is the conventional terminal). Registration order is chain order and the DI container plays the handler-factory role, so the classic hierarchy is not needed. Write middleware inline as a delegate or as a reusable class with an `InvokeAsync(HttpContext, RequestDelegate)` method.
pitfalls: Calling next.Invoke after the response has started throws - check context.Response.HasStarted before writing.
Middleware registered after a Run delegate never executes; the mistake is silent until a request hits the missing stage.
Capturing a scoped service in a singleton middleware breaks DI lifetimes; inject per-request services through InvokeAsync parameters instead.

variants.name: Classic GoF Handler with successor property
variants.idiom_name: abstract Handler class with a Successor property and Handle()
variants.implementation_notes: Outside ASP.NET - desktop apps, background services, in-process command handling - the classic structure still applies: an abstract Handler with a `Successor` property and a `Handle(request)` method, concrete handlers that return a result or forward, and an explicit terminal handler. It is hand-written but needs no ownership handling, unlike C++. In modern C# the delegate form (`Func<Request, bool>` or `Func<Request, Response?>` chains, possibly with nullable reference types) is usually shorter, so keep the class hierarchy for handlers that need identity, injected state or runtime rewiring.
pitfalls: Treating a missing Successor as a normal outcome hides a missing terminal handler; return an explicit unhandled result instead of null.
A chain shared across concurrent requests must not have its Successor rewritten at runtime; build it once at startup.
Nullable-reference-type warnings about Successor are usually a design signal, not noise to suppress.
